title: Maximum of Two Numbers
directAnswer: Return `a > b ? a : b`. A single comparison decides it; ties can return either value.

rules: Generalises to N values by folding a running max.
remember.takeaway: Master the ternary here; you'll reuse it inside every running-max loop.
whenToUse: Choosing the larger of two values
The base step inside any running-max loop

problemStatement: Given two integers `a` and `b`, return the larger one.
understanding: Compare the two values and return whichever is bigger. If they're equal, either value is the 'maximum'.

approaches.name: Single comparison
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
The maximum of two values is decided by a **single comparison**: if `a` is larger, the answer is `a`; otherwise it is `b`. The ternary `a > b ? a : b` expresses exactly that in one expression.

**Why ties don't matter.** When `a == b`, both branches return the same numeric value, so it is irrelevant whether you use `>` or `>=` — the result is identical. Don't waste a branch worrying about equality.

**Why this matters beyond two numbers.** This one comparison is the *atom* of every 'running maximum' loop. Finding the max of an array is just this comparison applied repeatedly against an accumulator. Internalise the ternary here and the array version writes itself.

**On using the library `Math.max`.** It's correct and you'd use it in real code, but if the interviewer is testing fundamentals they want to see the comparison. Mention both: 'In production I'd call `Math.max`; here's the comparison it's doing under the hood.'

code.python:
def max_two(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a if a > b else b

hints: Only one fact decides the answer: is `a` bigger than `b`?
A single comparison with a ternary returns the larger value directly.
Don't add a separate branch for equality — both values are the same then.
approaches.complexityReasoning: exactly one comparison and one selection regardless of the operand sizes.

edgeCases.behavior: Equal — returns 4; the `>` test is false so it returns b, which is the same value.
Returns -2; comparisons work the same for negatives.

pitfalls: Over-engineering with if/else-if chains when one ternary suffices.
Believing the `>` vs `>=` choice changes the result on a tie — it doesn't.

commonMistakes: Using `if/else if` but forgetting the equal case (still works, but shows fuzzy thinking).
Calling a library `max` when the interviewer wants to see the comparison.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can express a selection cleanly and recognise it as the base case of a running max.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Writing verbose nested ifs, or reaching for the library when asked to show the logic.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Point out this is exactly the comparison an array-maximum loop repeats n times.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should I return on a tie?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Either value — they're equal, so the result is the same number.
